passage: I'm Thomas. I sit behind Dolma in chemistry, and since the fire in her building last year, she's been different. I don't know what's going on inside her. I can only say what I see. When the fire drill bell rang in October, she didn't move. She sat completely still, staring at the desk, until our teacher touched her arm. Other times she's the opposite: she agrees to everything anyone asks. Lend a pen, do my homework, swap seats. She says "Sorry, sorry" even when someone bumps into her. Some people call her a pushover. Last week I heard the counsellor talking to her in the corridor. "Your body learnt to protect you, Dolma. Going still and keeping everyone happy were ways to stay safe. It's not a flaw in you." Dolma nodded, and for once she didn't say sorry.

qa.q: What did Dolma do when the fire drill bell rang?
qa.a: She didn't move; she sat completely still, staring at the desk.

qa.q: What does Dolma saying 'Sorry, sorry' when someone bumps her suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels anxious and unsafe, as if she has to keep everyone happy to stay safe, even when she did nothing wrong.

qa.q: How did the counsellor's words reframe Dolma's behaviour?
qa.a: The counsellor explained that freezing and pleasing everyone are ways her body learned to protect her, not flaws.

qa.q: How might the people who call Dolma a pushover see her if they heard the counsellor?
qa.a: They might see that her agreeing to everything is a protective reaction after a frightening event, not weakness.

grounding: A classmate sees a teenager who freezes and pleases everyone after a frightening fire, and hears these explained as protective survival responses, not character faults.

passage: March. Two months after Farhan was attacked on his way home from tuition, a classmate grabbed his shoulder from behind as a joke. Farhan spun and shoved him into the desks. The class went silent. He was sent to the principal, shaking. April. In a maths test, a door slammed down the corridor. Before he knew it, Farhan was outside the school gate, running, heart pounding. He didn't remember deciding to leave. May. Ms. Vidya, the school counsellor, drew three stick figures for him: one fighting, one running, one frozen. "When something frightening happens, your body learns to protect you. It reacts before your thinking brain catches up. That's not a bad character, Farhan. It's survival." Farhan stared at the drawing a long time. "So I'm not a violent person." "No. You're a person who got hurt. And we can work on this together."

qa.q: What did Ms. Vidya draw for Farhan?
qa.a: Three stick figures: one fighting, one running, one frozen.

qa.q: What was Farhan afraid his reactions said about him?
qa.a: He feared they meant he was a violent person.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Farhan understood himself?
qa.a: Ms. Vidya explained that his shoving and running were survival responses, not a bad character.

qa.q: How might the classmate who grabbed him see the shove differently if he knew the reason?
qa.a: He might understand it was a protective reaction to being startled after an attack, not plain aggression.

grounding: It shows a teenager who lashes out and runs after a frightening attack, and learns these are protective survival responses, not character faults.

passage: Aadhya, you asked why I was so weird after the accident. Okay. I'm Farhan, and last year a car hit my cycle at the crossing near school. I wasn't badly hurt, but after that, whenever I reached a crossing, I just froze. Couldn't move. Other times, if someone bumped me in the corridor, I'd shout at them, and once I pushed a guy. And with teachers I became super polite, agreeing to everything, like if I kept everyone happy nothing bad could happen. I thought I'd turned into a bad person. The school counsellor explained that freezing, fighting and pleasing people are ways the body tries to stay safe after something scary. They're not who you are. That changed everything for me.

qa.q: Where did the car hit Farhan's cycle?
qa.a: At the crossing near school.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel about the reactions before seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: Farhan felt ashamed and confused, believing that meant becoming a bad person.

qa.q: What helped Farhan understand those reactions?
qa.a: The school counsellor explained that freezing, lashing out and pleasing people are the body's ways of trying to stay safe, not character faults.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have seen Farhan after the accident?
qa.a: Aadhya probably found Farhan strange and unpredictable, not knowing the reactions came from the fear of the accident.

grounding: Shows a teenager who freezes, lashes out and people-pleases after a frightening accident, and learns these are protective survival responses, not faults.

passage:
Monday: Three weeks after the flood swept through their colony, Vishal, fifteen, sat in class staring at nothing. The teacher called his name twice. He didn't hear.
Thursday: At lunch, Deepak grabbed Vishal's shoulder from behind as a joke. Vishal spun and shoved him hard into the bench. "Don't touch me!" Everyone went quiet. Vishal ran out of the gate and didn't come back till evening.
The next Tuesday: The school counsellor had met Vishal twice. She explained that going numb, lashing out and running are the body's alarms after a terrifying night, not proof he was bad. That afternoon Vishal found Deepak. "I'm sorry. It wasn't you. Since the flood, I jump at everything." Deepak nodded slowly. "I didn't know. I'll stop grabbing."

qa.q: What did Vishal shout when Deepak grabbed him?
qa.a: He shouted "Don't touch me!"

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when Deepak grabbed his shoulder?
qa.a: He felt suddenly terrified and threatened, so he shoved Deepak and ran.

qa.q: What helped Vishal make things right with Deepak?
qa.a: The counsellor helped him see his reactions as survival alarms, not bad character, which gave him words to explain and apologise.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when Vishal apologised?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt relieved and understanding, realising the shove was not really about him.

grounding: Shows a teenager who goes numb, lashes out and runs after a frightening flood, and learns these are protective survival responses, not character faults.

passage: "Varun, you pushed your friend yesterday and then hated yourself for it, na? Sit. When I was fifteen, there was a robbery in our house at night. Nobody was hurt, but after that I became the most helpful girl in the world. I agreed with everyone. I said yes to every teacher, every aunty, every friend. Never angry, never tired. People called me such a good girl. But inside I was always frightened, like if I made everyone happy, nothing bad could happen again. Years later a counsellor told me that pleasing everyone was my way of staying safe, like some people freeze or fight. It was not a flaw. So your pushing, beta, I understand. Your Jaya Bua will help you find someone to talk to."

qa.q: What happened in Jaya's house when she was fifteen?
qa.a: There was a robbery in the house at night.

qa.q: How did young Jaya feel inside while pleasing everyone?
qa.a: She felt constantly frightened, believing that keeping everyone happy would stop anything bad from happening.

qa.q: What turning point helped Jaya understand herself?
qa.a: A counsellor explained that pleasing everyone was a survival response to feel safe, not a flaw.

qa.q: How might the people around young Jaya have seen her?
qa.a: They saw her as a good, helpful girl, without knowing she was scared inside.

grounding: An elder recalls becoming a people-pleaser after a frightening robbery, learning it was a protective survival response rather than a character fault.

passage:
It had been two months since the school bus accident, and exam week had come with pouring rain. Farhan and Naveen had both been on that bus.
In the exam hall, a truck horn blared outside. Farhan froze, pen stopped mid-word, eyes blank. He didn't hear the invigilator call his name.
Naveen jumped too, but differently. When a classmate joked, "Scared of a horn?" Naveen shoved him hard and was sent out.
At home Farhan had become the perfect son, agreeing to everything, never saying no. His mother thought he was fine.
That Friday the school counsellor met both boys. "Freezing, going numb, lashing out, trying to please everyone, these are ways your body tried to keep you safe," she said. "They're not signs that you're bad or weak." Naveen looked up, surprised. Farhan's shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What sound made Farhan freeze in the exam hall?
qa.a: A truck horn blaring outside.

qa.q: How was Farhan feeling in the exam hall?
qa.a: He was frightened and went numb, frozen and blank, not even hearing his name.

qa.q: What did the counsellor explain that could help both boys?
qa.a: That freezing, lashing out and pleasing everyone are protective survival responses after something frightening, not character faults.

qa.q: How might Farhan's mother see him differently after learning this?
qa.a: She might realise that his constant agreeing was a way of staying safe, not proof that he was fine.

grounding: After a bus accident, Farhan freezes, goes numb and pleases everyone while Naveen lashes out, and a counsellor explains these are survival responses, not faults.
